speechtext:
On February 10 the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) asked the following question:
May I ask the Prime Minister what commitments, if any, have been made by Canada with regard to imperial defence?
I answered at the time:
I would have to have a conference with my colleague the Minister of Defence before I could answer my hon. friend. I am not aware of any commitments, myself, at the moment.
I now give my hon. friend the answer, having taken up the matter with the Minister of National Defence:
While declarations on behalf of Canada on the subject of the defence of Canada have been made at various imperial conferences, as may be seen from the results thereof published from time to time, I am not aware of any commitments made on behalf of Canada with regard to imperial defence. At such conferences it has been expressly recognized that it is for the parliaments of the several parts of the British commonwealth of nations, upon the recommendation of their respective governments, to decide upon their course.

speechtext: May I reply, Mr. Speaker, to a question asked last evening by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) as to the distribution of the Canada-United States trade agreement. speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that is not the point I had in mind. I had in mind the supplying of information that would enable a proper discussion of the agreement to be had in this chamber. It will be recalled that when the British agreements were under consideration, and the agreements made with other parts of the British empire, we printed for the use of members a complete record of the tariffs and changes, showing what the tariff rates were and what the changes were. Inasmuch as the right hon. gentleman has indicated that the agreement contemplates a great alteration in the whole tariff structure of the country, it might foe desirable, in fact it is desirable, that there should be in the hands of hon. members a statement showing what the existing tariff rates are that will be applicable to the United States, and what the United States tariff rates are that will be made applicable to Canada on the various items that are affected by the agreement in both countries. That is the information that was received by the house when the imperial trade agreements were under consideration; and it does seem to me that, in order that the agreement may be properly studied, such things should be available to the members of the house in convenient form. I think on that occasion we did circulate a copy of the whole tariff act, and supplied also several sheets that contained comparisons between the existing rates and the rates that were to come into force under the agreement.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last evening I was pointing out that the speech from the throne had entirely overlooked certain elements in our population, not the least of which were those now facing dire poverty and distress on the western prairies. I was on the point of observing that in the district immediately surrounding the city of Weybum alone we distributed last winter over two hundred babies' layettes where children h^d been born into the world to families without fitting garments in which to clothe them. It was not an unusual thing to find new bom children clad in garments made from washed-out flour sacks. I draw these facts to the attention of the house because I believe those people have been totally overlooked in the deliberations of the present administration.
I should like also to draw to the attention of the house some other elements in our population that I think have been

The Address-Mr. Douglas

neglected as far as the speech from the throne would indicate. First I would direct attention to the large farming population. The income of the farmers, particularly those of the west but also those of all Canada, has declined steadily during the last five years, with the result that to-day the best authorities tell us that the average farm income is about $350 per year, and I know many who are living on less. The cost of living and the cost of farm operation have not declined accordingly. The fixing of the price of wheat last summer by the late administration helped a great deal, more I think than they were given credit for, but I want to suggest to the present administration that we need to go further. I would particularly direct the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to two things that need to be done if we are to help western agriculture. The first is to have that fixed price apply to all grains as well as to wheat; the second is to have that fixed price made retroactive. I know of an instance, and it is not uncommon, of a man who sold his entire wheat crop under economic pressure just six days before the price of wheat was pegged, with the result that he lost eleven cents per bushel on a fairly large crop. But there are farmers who had no crop at all, and who did not get the benefit of this fixed price. At the present time they are faced with appalling conditions. I can remember sitting in an audience in the city of Estevan and listening to the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) suggest that he was in favour of some type of crop insurance. I have read the speech from the throne again and again but I fail to find any indication that we are to have crop insurance or anything else that will take care of the economic insecurity of those who, through drought, grasshoppers and other whims of nature, find themselves deprived of their livelihood.
But, Mr. Speaker, there is another circumstance that is oppressing the agricultural community; that is the tremendous burden of debt that hangs about the necks of the farmers. The figures for last year show that the farm mortgage indebtedness of the Dominion of Canada is more than $671,000,000, while for the three prairie provinces it is $324,000,000. On July 1, 1932, the farm management department of the university of Saskatchewan published a statement edited by professors Allen and Hope concerning Scott municipality, which happens to be in my constituency. These gentlemen showed that there were eighty-four farm-owners in that municipality; that the average1 acreage

of these farms was 628 acres and that the average debt against each farm was $14,700. In many cases that is a great deal more than the farms could have been sold for at that time, or even at this. .
Of these debts eighty per cent were incurred when wheat was $2 or more per bushel. Today these people are trying to meet their obligations with wheat at 87^ cents or less, because many of them had only a feed wheat crop last year. Therefore I direct the attention of the government to the fact that the speech from the throne contains no adequate solution of the problem confronting this great agricultural community, that is looking to this house for some type of assistance at this time.
Then I would direct the attention of the house to the fact that across Canada there is a great army of unemployed, with over a million people living on some type of government assistance or relief. What does the speech from the throne suggest that the government is prepared to do for this army of peoplfe? It suggests that we are to have a national unemployment commission. I have read the words, " They asked for bread and they were given a stone." The unemployed of this country have asked for bread and they have been given a commission. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it is not commissions and supervision we need; what we need is to deal with the fundamental economic issue of the reorganization of our economic system in order to put purchasing power back into the pockets of the common people to enable them to buy back the things they produce. I suggest that these fundamental issues are not being met. What about unemployment insurance; what about the work and wages program about which the Liberal party have spoken so frequently in the past? The people of this country are asking about this; they want to know.
Then I would direct your attention, sir, to another class of people, men and women between sixty and seventy years of age, the people who produced the wealth of this country, who helped build the Dominion of Canada to all that it is to-day. Thousands of them have come to the place where they can no longer face the future with any degree of optimism. Large industries are no longer hiring them; many of them, salesman, commercial travellers, technicians, have been cast aside like a squeezed out orange rind.- What do we propose to do for them? They produced the wealth of the country. I maintain that they have the right to a share in it. I maintain that legislation should be placed on our statute books to take care of men and

The Address-Mr. Douglas
women who, having served their day and generation faithfully and well, now look to society to do its part in giving to them a measure of economic security.
I should like to draw the attention of the house to the plight of the great class of merchants throughout Canada. I hold in my hand an excerpt from a Saskatchewan newspaper reporting a telegram sent by the present Prime Minister to some of his constituents in Prince Albert, in which he said:
I approve wholeheartedly of their recommendations in reference to report of price spreads commission.
From that I took it that the Prime Minister was opposed to rebates and discounts, to these unfair trade practices by which large mail order houses and chain stores have gradually and ruthlessly been driving down the business of the small merchants, yet in the speech from the throne I find nothing to indicate that concrete measures are to be placed upon our statute books to meet that situation. Are we to infer that the rule of laissez faire is to continue? Darwin said that the law,of the jungle is the survival of the fittest; I wonder if my hon. friends think the law of economics is the survival of the slickest. One would gather that, as one sees the very noticeable absence of any legislation in this respect.
I draw attention to the fact that across this dominion there are thousands of exsoldiers, burnt-outs, men who gave the best years of their lives in the great war, men who to-day are partly or wholly incapacitated in the race of life. They want to know what a grateful country-at -least vocally grateful-is prepared to do for them now that they are no longer able to do anything for themselves. Some fine recommendations were made by a commission called the Iiyndman commission; what does the government propose to do about those recommendations? I think the house has a right to know.
One of the most crying problems facing the Canadian people in all parts of this dominion is the tremendous one of public health. People need dental and medical and hospital care. We have all the facilities for rendering those services, yet there is not an hon. member who does not know that people who have money can secure those services and people who have not money cannot, and are not getting them.

My hon. friend says it is not so. But we know that to be true on the prairies, and there is no doubt it is true in 12739-94
other parts of Canada. While doctors and dentists have given of themselves until some of them are almost bankrupt, many people have had to go without the necessary dental care, the necessary medical care, have had to stay at home and have treatment in their homes, simply because they have not the money. I am not saying this condition can be rectified overnight, but I suggest that the dominion government take immediate steps to formulate a co-ordinated health policy for the Dominion of Canada. The greatest asset of the country is the health and welfare of her people, and that should be the first consideration of any government.
I am most interested in the problem of youth. It was a move in the right direction when the relief camps were transferred from the Department of National Defence to the Department of Labour. I read with something of amusement that these camps are to be abolished at an early date "as expanding employment opportunities permit." In other words, as business absorbs these young men the camps will be abolished. Of course when business absorbs these young men the camps will not be needed. But that is not meeting the problem at all. What we need is the abolition of these camps; what we need is to place these young men in gainful employment and wholesome environment. In the report of the commission of inquiry, excerpts from which appeared in the press last week, we find them lamenting the subversive influences found in these camps. Let me say that there are other influences more subversive, for instance, the demoralizing influence upon young men of seeing the years go by and finding themselves without technical training or mental preparation for useful work, with the result that even if conditions do right themselves these young men will find that their places have been taken by those better skilled and younger than they are. There is the problem.
Last night the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) very proudly displayed some campaign literature. I do not know that it is . worth while in an assembly like this to spend our time metaphorically thumbing our noses back and forth across the floor. But I would like to draw attention to some campaign literature that the people of Canada have not forgotten: "Jobs or doles, which? Vote Liberal." "Vote Liberal and get back from the poorhouse." "Tory policies cannot end unemployment; vote Liberal."

Mr. Speaker, may I first
of all congratulate you, sir, upon your election t,o the high office of Speaker of the House of Commons. May I also join with those who extended congratulations to the hon. members who so ably moved and seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
It is not my intention to discuss the various matters to which reference is made in the speech from the throne. But it seems to me advisable and necessary that some reply should be made to the speech made by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) in relation to the question of wheat. I desire to deal as briefly as I can with some of the inaccuracies in that speech, some of the inferences with which I cannot agree, some even of the insinuations which I regard as unjust and unfair, made against a man and against men who have no opportunity here to defend themselves; and to say something with regard to the amazing attack-I would almost say the malicious attack- which was made upon the present chairman of the wheat board. I would conclude with a discussion of the method by which the members of the farmer wheat 'board -were relieved of office, and finally, and most important of all, I wish to place on record the policy of the present government with regard to the wheat question so that the House of Commons and the country itself may not be misled.
This problem of the disposal of the wheat surplus of western Canada is no longer only a western problem. I am not saying anything to the detriment .of the western farmer; indeed I have every sympathy with him when I say that eastern Canada has now perhaps not quite so great but a very substantial interest in the disposal of the western wheat surplus. Millions of dollars-yes, scores of millions of dollars are at stake in the operations carried on by the former government in connection with the accumulation and sale of wheat through Mr. McFarland and the

wheat board, and the possible and probable losses must be borne by the whole country.
On Monday the right hon. gentleman made some references to certain rumours going about to the detriment of Mr. McFarland. I do not propose to pay any attention to them. He spoke about the blasted reputations of the men who were relieved of their duties as members of the old wheat board. Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to cover a very great deal of ground on this occasion, first, for the very clear and definite reason that, instead of three and a half or four hours in which to speak I have only forty minutes. The other reason is this:	I have but one
thought to which I wish to give expression to-day, and I will reserve for other occasions the discussion on various subjects that naturally come to one's mind. During this session I think there will be ample opportunity to discuss many matters of vital interest to this country, so if I do not mention them to-day it is not because I am lacking in any appreciation of their significance or their importance at the present time.
The government has come into office with an unusually strong support in this house. It is no false flattery for me to say that the government should be congratulated upon the expression of confidence that has been accorded it by the people of Canada. Any government or any party might well be proud of that expression of confidence, but at the same time I would suggest to the government and particularly, shall I say, to the new members of the Liberal party who are supporting the government in the house, that Canada is expecting great things from this government and this parliament, dominated and controlled as it is by the Liberal party. As far as I am concerned, in reference to any measures calculated to advance the interests of the people of Canada, I shall very gladly and freely cooperate with the government in passing such measures. I repeat, however, that the country expects much of the government. I would rather say, if I might do so without offence, that I think the country expects much of this parliament and I wish to start this session, as far as I am concerned, with the suggestion that it is parliament, the House of Commons, that should assert itself rather than that we should focus too much attention upon the administration, and I do not say that with the slightest sense of disrespect to the administration.
Before addressing myself to the matters with which I wish to deal, I should like to
indulge for just a moment in what was indulged in by the leaders of the two major parties, that is, a little playing around with percentages. It is about the only comfort I can take out of the situation and I propose at once to arrogate to myself that modicum of comfort. I have made an analysis of the vote and I find that the Liberal party polled 2,061,000 votes, which means that each Liberal member in the House of Commons represents, on an average, 11,500 voters. Each Conservative member represents, on an average, 32,000 voters *-not so bad, as someone says, and I quite agree. My Social Credit friends represent, on an average, 10,750 votes-not so bad again. Each Cooperative Commonwealth Federation member represents an average of 55,000 votes. The members of the Reconstruction party, however, each represent an average of 384,000 voters. So, Mr. Speaker when it comes to playing around with aver ages and percentages in connection with the voting, at least I can claim to be in rather a unique position. I think I am entitled to say-and I say it this once-that I am conscious of a very great responsibility in speaking for that large number of voters, though certainly in a numerical way I do not count for very much in this house of 245 members, a house in which I have been sitting for twenty-five years, so that I know something of its constitution, its habits and its practices; but, sir, I have a large measure of pride in the fact that I can speak for a large body of the free citizens of this country.
We met this year under a shadow, that of the death of a beloved sovereign. I think King George will be remembered through the ages and will be portrayed on the pages of history not only as a sovereign beloved by his people but also, I think, as one having the further unique record that in practically every Country not belonging to the empire he was respected and admired. I had hoped, Mr. Speaker, that, meeting under the spell of this sad but inspiring circumstance, we in this parliament might forget partisan feelings and differences, unite in an effort to study the welfare and promote measures for the general well-being of this country, and contribute to the solution of our common problems. This, sir, is the House of Commons.
May I digress for a moment to say a word to that very large body of menibers who sit in parliament for the first time. I have not checked the figures with care, but I am told, sir, Ithat there are more new members in this parliament than ever sat in any new parliament since confederation. That may

not be correct, but it is certainly true that there is a very large number of members here who never sat in parliament before and, of course, the great majority of them sit with the Liberal party. It has occurred to me since the election, and since the house met, that a great many Liberal members who sit for the first time in this parliament have come here earnestly imbued with the doctrines, the old, ancient doctrines, of their party. I am going to offer a word of warning; it is this-and I speak from a recollection of my own entry into the House of Commons twenty-five years ago-you come to the house convinced that your great party-the Liberal party I shall .address for the moment

stands for what you believe to be best in the political life of the community. You come here with a conviction that you as an individual will be able to contribute something to the solution of your nation's problems. And you wall be, unless you fall under the spell of extreme partisanship and allow your better judgment, your convictions and your conscience to be dominated by the exigencies of the party whip. I am not saying that with any disrespect to the new chief whip of the Liberal party, a gentleman whom I respect and admire and whom I count as a friend. But it is part of the game. I venture to say thaJt there is not an older member in the house on either side but looks back over the years and recalls that time after time he has subjugated his own best judgment to what was conceived to be for the moment the good of the political fortunes of his party. Now it does not necessarily follow-and I say this with some knowledge and experience-that a man must always separate himself from his party, but he can make himself heard and felt in the house, in debate, and in the party caucus if you wish, make his views known, his influence felt when he knows and is convinced that something proposed is not in the best interests of the community as a whole. I would plead with the house, not necessarily to break away from party, but, at least in these years of adversity and struggle, to endeavour to bring to the service of the country what is in the interests of the country and not simply in the party interest.
I said a moment ago that this is the House of Commons. It is not the house of privileged interests; it is not the house of power. We often hear about accession to power, as if mere accession to power gave some divine right to do anything you wish. That is not so. This is the house of the common people of Canada. It is often referred to as the high court of parliament; personally I do not like the term. Not but what it is in a sense true,

but when it is used over and over again it seems to carry with it the inference that only a student of the law has any right to a voice in this house. This is not the high court in that sense; this is a forum for the common people, where their representatives may express their views; where, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has so often said, their rights and their privileges may be safeguarded. And the first duty of every member who comes into the house is to preserve to himself and herself the rights of those whom they represent, irrespective of what may be said by those who consider it to be other than a forum of the common people. Thank heaven, Mr. Speaker, that Canada is still a democracy, at least in name if not in fact. I think we might well pause to consider that. Let us ask: What is a democracy? I ran across a quotation from Kant, the philosopher; he used these words, indicating how a democracy should function, and I commend them to the attention of hon. members:
So to act as to treat humanity as an end and' never as a means.
That is, a democratic institution like this parliament should at. all times so act that whatever it does has in view the welfare of humanity before the welfare of special interests, and never think of or treat the individual as a means to an end. That philosopher was not a Christian, but in those words he epitomizes the very essence of Christian teaching as it relates to human beings.
Slavery is a denial of democracy. Slavery is a denial of freedom. It is an absence of freedom. I ask the house: Is there freedom in Canada to-day? Let us pause and ponder. One has but to read the history of politics in Great Britain, in the mother of parliaments, and in Canada and elsewhere, and one must recognize in fairness and justice that the Liberal party have made great contributions to political liberty. I remember hearing an eminent authority saying not long ago that there were 5,000,000 deposit accounts in Canada, and the statement was made as evidence to prove that the great masses of the people had savings accounts. Well, I know this:	I
checked up at one factory, and although it is very difficult to get them to talk I found that out of 250 workers only twelve had bank accounts. Upon making a further check I found dozens of concerns having ten and twelve bank accounts which did not represent individuals. Practically every church in Canada has bank accounts for the board of trustees, the board of management, the missionary society, the Sunday school, the young people's society, and so on. There may be ten or twelve accounts in all. Yet we hear the statement made that there are 5,000,000 deposit accounts in Canada; I question if there are 2,000,000. Nobody knows. The point is that we do know there is no sense of security in employment, and as a result there is no economic freedom or liberty.

speechtext: Is this condition peculiar to Canada?

speechtext:
Not at all. In fact, I believe Canada is perhaps more blessed in that regard than is any other country, and to a greater extent than is the United States.
I am glad the question has been asked, because it forms the basis of an observation to which I should like to give expression, if I have time, that it is in the 'hands of this parliament in the series of sessions held this year, next year, the next, and so on, to pass those measures which will lay the foundation in Canada for economic freedom, for democracy and for the establishment of this great realm. Where? On the basis of the welfare of the agriculturist and the worker. If it does not rest there, then there can be no security for the so-called upper strata.
The Address-Mr. Stevens

I wish to impress this fact upon parliament, although it may not be heeded: We hear a great deal of discussion about the constitutionality of this or that law. At the present time eight acts of parliament are before the supreme court awaiting decision as to their constitutionality. I am strongly convinced that if the parliament of Canada will speak firmly for the Canadian people, and the rights and interests of those people, we shall not need very much law. May I illustrate that point. Two years ago the price spreads committee sat in this building, and before it appeared one of the greatest corporations in Canada, the Imperial Tobacco Company. The facts disclosed that that company had cut the price of tobacco from around 30 cents per pound to from 14 to 16 cents per pound. They had reduced wages by a substantial percentage. They had imposed certain conditions upon retailers and had paid exorbitant bonuses to their executive officers. Those facts, and some information as to capital structure, were disclosed by the committee. What happened? Company officials appeared reluctantly, and at first I believe were very much annoyed in having the facts spread out. They were spread out, however, before the public of Canada. What happened? Almost immediately after the close of that session of parliament the Imperial Tobacco Company amended its buying policy. Hon. members from Essex, Elgin and other counties in western Ontario will know that I am stating the truth. Last year and the year before they restored the price of tobacco to from 27 to 30 cents per pound, thereby changing the state of the growers from that of abject poverty in 1932 and 1933 to comparative prosperity in 1934 and 1935. Next they restored the wages of their employees and, moreover, inaugurated a system of pensions and health benefits for them. They went further; they made new agreements with the retailers on an equitable and fair basis. All of that was done voluntarily-no law, no compulsion-only with knowledge of the fact that a committee of parliament had looked at and had permitted the public to look at the picture. That is what may result from a position parliament may take in connection with some of these matters. '
When a week or so ago the government of the day took up the challenge of a great corporation which had closed its doors and turned its employees out on the street, what happened? They opened their doors. Why? Because public opinion would not tolerate such a situation. Do not let the house disregard the influence and power which parliament has, not by interfering in business, not 
by trying to run business, but by standing as the impartial umpire between selfish and unscrupulous interests and corporations on the one hand and those who suffer from their operations on the other. Let parliament stand as the champion of the rights of the common people, as the House of Commons by its very name indicates it is, and we shall see a great change. But there must be a clear-cut, forceful and definite expression of determination on -the part of hon. members that these conditions shall not exist. Let them declare for a fair price to the farmer. I do not believe there is an hon. member in this chamber who knows better than I do the perplexities, difficulties and dangers involved in fixing prices. I am not asking for the moment that we fix prices, but I am asking parliament to declare, as one of the fundamental principles upon which the economic structure of this country was based, that fair prices shall be paid to the farmers, that body which forms one-half of our population. I ask that parliament shall declare, as an underlying principle of the economic life of this country, that fair wages shall be paid to the wage earner. I may be told that that is just a pious expression of opinion, but if parliament will bring before it those matters that do violence to the two principles I have mentioned, it will be found that employing authorities will try .to conform to the view that parliament thus expresses.
Another point which I wish to emphasize is this: If we are to revive business in this country and relieve unemployment and all the other distresses that are prevalent in Canada to-day, we must take some action that will raise the purchasing power of the masses of the people. The hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas), speaking a few moments ago, outlined some of the conditions that he had seen in the west. I recall, Mr. Speaker, a trip that I made when I was electioneering in the constituency of the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. MacMillan) in 1933; he will recall meeting me there. I addressed some forty-seven meetings; I met literally thousands of farmers; I went on some of their farms and into some of their homes and I saw the conditions obtaining in that district. Then I went into northern Alberta and there I saw conditions such as my hon. friend described a moment ago in somewhat different form- many and many a home, I venture to say thousands of homes, where there was lack of clothing, and I was told by dozens and dozens that their children because of lack of clothing could not leave their door until the warm spring weather came. And that, Mr. Speaker,

The Address-Mr. Stevens
is in Canada where we know the great, the dominating proportion of the farming community is not getting a return to-day sufficient to provide those people with warm clothing, and decent blankets for their beds, let alone furniture. Raise their purchasing power. Increase the returns to the farmer, and when you have raised their purchasing power you will stimulate the production of goods for consumption in this country and thus contribute more to the rapid relief of unemployment than could be done in any other way, whether it be in the manufacture of clothing, boots and shoes, furniture, farm machinery, houses and so forth. These are the things that are necessary, but before that comes you must give to the farming community of Canada a reasonable purchasing power.

Wait a minute. That light laugh is one of the things that makes me despair of parliament. I say to my friends on *the government benches: Let them take the quotations which the hon. member for Lethbridge gave from their Prime Minister's speech, and not his views but the authorities he quoted, and they cannot but be impressed by the seriousness of this whole business. Let us at least try to get down to the fundamental principles underlying it all, and then whether the hon. member for Lethbridge has the solution or whether hon. gentlemen opposite have it, let us all work together to find a common solution. I am not willing to accept my hon. friend's doctrines yet. I want to be shown some things first, but I do say this, that credit and the control of credit lie very near the root of the tremble.
People in this country have been calling for the opportunity to work, but, Mr. Speaker, there is a strange condition developing right in this country and in the United States. I was in Toronto the other day and a manufacturer told me that he was having difficulty in getting skilled workers in his plant. I read an editorial in the Toronto Globe a day or two ago, on February 10, which is rather startling. It says:
At a conference recently of business leaders in Chicago it was stated that, though hundreds of jobs calling for technical knowledge were opening, trained men could not be found to fill them.
It goes on:
This scarcity was described as most acute in the automobile and general machine trades, though it was experienced by industry in general.
Yet why should the condition be startling? Its roots may be found further back than the beginning of the depression. In the heyday of prosperity youth rather scorned the overalls occupations, and took to the white-collar jobs. There was plenty of money to be made; so why toil all day in machine shops? Trade apprenticeships did not appeal. When the depression came industry slowed down; so did everything else, and there wern't so many either white-collar or overalls jobs. There were fewer opportunities for learning trades; boys were not needed, and staffs were being reduced. Many aging mechanics, idle for five years, have grown too old to resume their former hard work. The consequence is that, with a revival of industry, there is no adequate supply of trained workers.
The Address-Mr. Stevens

Is it not startling and challenging to this parliament that., with the stimulation of industrial activity, there is now developing in Canada as well as in the United States a situation where there is actually a scarcity of trained men, when we have hundreds of thousands of unemployed? It is all very well for industrialists and great commercial leaders to tell politicians to keep their hands off business, but here is something which challenges the business leaders as well as parliament, and in my opinion we dare not as a parliament ignore this situation.' I should like to ask: Why should not a university graduate in mechanical engineering put on overalls and work at a machine? Is the legal profession more honourable than the calling of the machinist? Is the financier more noble as a man than is a carpenter? Cannot we in Canada get .away from the idea that there is something inferior about a man working with his hands? I might ask this question: Is it coming to this in Canada that we are going to develop, if we have not done so already, a system of castes similar in effect to the castes of India, although they may be in another form? Is it to be that the workmen of Canada are to become the untouchables of Canada? I hope not. But unless parliament builds its policies-I am not talking about party policies; I am speaking of parliament -upon the foundations I have indicated, namely, the well-being of the great farming class and the working class, then the superstructure that we have erected will be insecure and in my opinion will topple and collapse sooner o.r later.
I should like to turn to some statistics which are published by the government, but I shall not go into them in great detail. These are analyses of income taxes made by the bureau of statistics, and any hon. member can obtain them. I shall not give all the figures but simply indicate certain percentages. During the five year period, 1930 to 1934 inclusive, the income of agrarians dropped 52 per cent. Earnings of retail merchants dropped 53 per cent in the same period, while those of wholesale merchants dropped 50 per cent. Earnings of manufacturers dropped 40 per cent, while earnings from natural resources, which include mining, dropped 17 per cent. Earnings of transportation and public utilities, which are closely allied to the producing and distributing elements, dropped 46 per cent. Earnings of all the producing elements decreased; farmers, industrialists, transportation, merchants, all experienced a diminution in income. But there is one class left, the financial. I find that the great financial group 
experienced in the same period an increase of 20 per cent. This is not a matter of someone saying: Oh, well, there is Stevens again attacking the bankers and the financial institutions. That is not the point at all. Wealth is produced by those who work in the soil, whether they be farmers or lumbermen, or those who work in the mines. It has to be produced out of the soil. What is capital? It is nothing more or less than what is left over after you have paid for the cost of producing real wealth and is available for reinvestment. That has been accumulating and has come under the control of a smaller and smaller number of corporations and persons. The point at issue in Canada is this:	Whereas there has been
an increase in the earnings of the great financial group, those who produce wealth, or create wealth, if you like to use that term, have all experienced a diminution in earnings. How long can this go on? Let any logical or impartial man give the answer to that question. Of one thing I am convinced, it cannot go on indefinitely.
In case it may be suggested that I have rather stretched this theme, let me quote from a speech made the other day by Sir Edward Beatty. Sir Edward made the very definite statement that more production is the remedy for unemployment. That is a rather striking statement from Sir Edward Beatty and I agree with it. I do not believe in the so-called doctrine of scarcity; I never had faith in it and never did believe in it. Let me quote Sir Edward as follows:
Men who came from farms, attracted by high wages paid by business institutions in the cities, and then abandoned to unemployment, had a legitimate cause for complaint against the skill with which private business is conducted.
Those are not my words; they are those of Sir Edward Beatty. That is no utterance of mine. In making that statement Sir Edward Beatty reflected what I believe is the conviction of every thoughtful student of modern business and economic problems. It is not sufficient for business men to warn governments and politicians to keep out of business. The long and short of the matter is the fact that the collapse of 1929 followed a period when private business was uninterrupted and unmeddled with, if I may use that term, by governments. My hon. friends will be the first to endorse that. Is Mr. Speaker going to call me to time?

The Address-Mr. Graydon

must be dealt with in detail later on, as it affects the fruit and vegetable men in the southern part of the riding which I represent. I am hopeful that' the expressions in the speech from the throne do not mean that seasonal regulations and dumping duties will not be available for the protection of the farmers whom I have the honour to represent.
I am not going to take up the time of the house by a lengthy address; in the county from which I come we believe in short sermons, short editorials, and short speeches. The man on the back concession, the workingman in the poor home, and the young man who is not able to find a job in this peculiar world, are watching eagerly the deliberations of this first session of the eighteenth parliament of Canada. I hope they will not be disappointed. They ask for leadership. They have been seeking it through many different channels. Let us hope that the leadership which will be provided by the government of our country will be of a quality which will be worth something to these three sections of the people; that it will actually amount to something beyond mere words; that words will be translated into concrete action looking to instant and permanent relief.
Therefore I say to the government of our country to-day, in all honesty and sincerity, that I do hope something along this line will be accomplished. I hope that their efforts will meet with the success that they themselves hope for; and I trust that our Conservative party, small in numbers though it may be, may play some definite and valuable part in assisting to bring to the Dominion of Canada the better times which you and I, Mr. Speaker, are so anxious to see prevail. I should like to offer the cooperation of one of the humblest private members in the house to the end that something practical may be done, and that mere partisanship shall not occupy the attention of the house to the extent that some who have voiced opinions suspect has been the case in the past. I hope we shall be able to throw aside in some degree party prejudices and do something for the man on the back concession, the workingman and his family, and the young men and women who have just come out

of school and are looking to the government of Canada to accomplish something worth while.
Mr. ELIE 0. BERTRAND (Prescott) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, at the outset of this session, I cannot, as a representative of the French Canadian minority in Ontario, refrain from expressing the grief felt by the people of this province at the death of our beloved sovereign George V. I wish to offer to His Gracious Majesty Edward VIII our deepest sympathy and also extend to Queen Mary and her family our sincerest condolences in their misfortune, to the new king a long reign, marked by peace and justice for all the citizens of the empire.
We are pleased to find in the speech from the throne the following paragraph with reference to the international situation.
The seriousness of the international situation has contributed to the world's anxieties. My ministers are confident that they express the convictions of the people of Canada in adhering to the aims and ideals of the League of Nations, and in seeking in unison with members of the league as well as with other nations to support by all appropriate and practical means the maintenance of peace and the establishment of a world order based on justice and equity.
The effect, sir, of the last war, our losses in men, the obligations we then assumed, the problem of pensions to veterans, our enormous war debt which is heavily burdening the Canadian people, all this obliges us to ponder seriously when a question of war crops up. On this score, I think we should, on behalf of our fellow citizens of Ontario, congratulate the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) for his admirable explanation of the Riddell motion at Geneva, in connection with sanctions against Italy on certain products, notably oil. The government is entitled to our congratulations on the attitude they took in this matter. Let our watchword be to avoid taking any responsibility regarding wars in foreign countries, and believe this will be a great step towards preserving peace all over the world.
Mr. Speaker, before going further, I wish to state that we of the Liberal party are highly pleased to congratulate you upon your appointment to the speakership. Your are eminently qualified for the high office you now occupy and the House will certainly benefit from your wide knowledge of parliamentary procedure and the fairplay which you have always shown during the many years when you were, so to speak, the guide of our party.
I wish to extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght),* who so ably moved the address in reply to the speech from the Throne. In a sound and

The Address-Mr. Bertrand
eloquent speech, he proclaimed the policy followed by our party and, he certainly did credit to the constituency which has just elected him. The entire representation of Ontario is proud to include within its ranks such a distinguished barrister.
I must also congradulate the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemon.t (Mr. Fournier) on his splendid debut in the House, as an orator. He reflected honour on his compatriots and will certainly he thie pride of his constituents.
I also deem it appropriate, sir, to congratulate the right hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King and his cabinet on the stupendous amount of work they have accomplished since the elections of October 14. We have already felt, in various parts of Canada, the benefit of the trade treaties concluded with certain foreign countries, notably with the United States. Carloads, even entire train-loads of cattle have already crossed the 45th parallel. The increased prices that have resulted to the producers have been a great boon to that portion of the farming community. Although we will not know before January, 1937, the tangible results of this trade treaty between Canada and the United States, which has been effective from the beginning of January, partial statistics are already available. In Alberta, the new trade regime was inaugurated by the shipping of a train-load of cattle at the beginning of January. Two other trains of 15 carloads have since been shipped. These are merely the most outstanding transactions; the treaty has also produced results in other domains for instance, in the prices of certain articles, even before it became effective.
This treaty was followed by a trade agreement with Japan which, imparting renewed activity to our lumber industry, provided employment to a large number of our workers.
Mr. W. R. Beatty, of Pembroke, Ont., who recently retired from the presidency of the Canadian Lumbermen's Association expressed himself as follows when presiding over the 28th annual convention of the Association, held recently at the Mount Royal hotel, in Montreal:
The newly-signed trade agreement between Canada and the United States will mean increased shipments to our friends to the south of us, according as recovery advances.
In normal times the United States need our lumber, and our lumber manufacturers need the American market; the treaty may gradually restore to us all of our lost markets. The renewed trade relations with Japan are also a reassuring promise, especially as regards the Pacific coast lumber industry which relies mostly on exports.
12739-10*
These are results which should rejoice us, they also prove that the Government's policy will find markets for the products which we cannot consume in Canada, and which must necessarily be sold abroad.
The speech from the throne also mentions unemployment, a national problem and one of the most pressing that faces the government. We were already aware that the government intended to allow more scope to the provinces and municipalities in this connection. This is confirmed in the speech from the throne it is stated that a federal commission comprising provincial and municipal representation will be created in order to study this problem prescribe remedies and find the best possible means of relieving the situation until the day when normal business recovery will entirely absorb the unemployed, who today number 400,000 but were far more numerous some time ago.
It is further stated that concentration camps will be broken up. All agree that these concentration camps should disappear at the earliest possible date.
The government would do well to take up such matters immediately and, with the cooperation of all interested parties, to find profitable work for the unemployed, as well as for those who are now in concentration camps.
Besides the agricultural problem to which I shall refer in a moment, we must take into consideration the large number of unemployed in this country. The government must not undertake to foster immigration to this country before the work and the development of our natural resources require it.
I wish to briefly broach the subject of amendments to the British North America Act. The question is certainly a very delicate one and we, the French Canadian minority, should give careful consideration to it. On more than an occasion and even on the floor of this house, the hard struggles which the French Canadians had to endure in order to safeguard their rights in Ontario have been discussed.
Some contend that the minorities of all country have had to undergo such struggles, that they are part of history throughout the various periods and that it will always be so. Nevertheless, the fact remains that, as a race, we certainly have our rights in this country and no amendment to the British North America Act must, in the future, prevent their recognition, both from the standpoint of religion and of nationality.
The speech from the throne goes on to say that necessary legislation will be brought
The Address

Mr. Bertrand

down in the course of this session to control credit and the issue of currency through the medium of the Bank of Canada. This is another delicate question; however, the Liberal party has already stated its policy in this regard, and we are proud to note that a bill will be introduced in the course of this session which will put this country in full control of our credit and of the issue of paper currency. This will perhaps prevent certain classes of our population to loudly proclaim, as they have been doing for some time past, that capital and wealth is created through the development of our natural resources and that this wealth could be easily distributed among all classes of society by the simple expedient of issuing paper currency. We must have faith in the future of our country and save it from bankruptcy. We must congratulate the government, which will, at the first opportunity, assume control of this credit, but it must not be to the benefit of certain classes only; it must be distributed equitably among all classes of the community.
It will certainly prove difficult to attain such an object, because every member of this house is aware of the large number of pamphlets, newspaper articles, editorials, resolutions from boards of trade, groups of business men and financial institutions of all kinds throughout the country which insist that parliament and the government find the necessary means to reduce expenses in a manner such as it has never been done before in the administration of our dominion or of any province. If such a policy was carried out, the people would be the first to suffer. Such are the means proposed to save the country. In all these resolutions we are urged to practise economy; but whom are we to ask to do so? Certainly not the unemployed, nor the workers whose wages are insufficient to give them a decent livelihood, nor the agricultural classes which are on the threshold of bankruptcy. Who shall be requested to practise such economy? The government simply provides the bare necessities of these people.
We know that the Liberal party has always been recognized as the party that has most practised economy, while safeguarding the interests of all classes of the country's population. We hear among the people such remarks as; You Liberals are always elected when the Conservative party has expended all the revenues of the country and there only remains for you to foot the bills. We are perhaps entitled to such an heritage which is certainly a compliment to the Liberal administration.

I cannot entirely agree with what the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) has just stated in connection with currency; however, it might perhaps be appropriate to point out, notwithstanding all the propaganda that is now carried on, that Canada is actually indebted to the extent of $3,000,000,000; moreover, she has guaranteed the liabilities of railway and other organizations to the amount of $1,600,000,000, while municipalities are indebted to the extent of $1,500,000,000, forming a total of $7,100,000,000 on which interest has to be met. Actually there are other liabilities for which the people are responsible for instance those of school boards and other public utilities. And we are urged in all the articles I have mentioned, to maintain the present rate of interest, to meet our obligations, to keep the country's credit intact, to avoid repudiating our debts and the guarantees we have given. Thrift is preached to those who are in want, in order to safeguard accumulated wealth by continuing to pay the same rates of interest. The average rate of interest on the total debt to which I have just referred amounts actually to 4i per cent. I base such figures on an article which appeared in "Saturday Night," entitled; Retrenchment, not conversion, the remedy. Note well that in this article it is absolutely urged that the 4J per cent rate of interest be maintained; it was even higher before certain conversions were carried out last year. By reducing the rate of interest to 3 per cent an amount of more than $100,000,000 would be economized yearly. This would mean a mere trifle which, according to these people, should be disregarded, because the word conversion would mean repudiation.
I must frankly confess, sir, in the face of conditions such as have been prevailing since two years, the working classes cannot live as comfortably as they did a few years ago owing to the lack of work; the farming class is passing through a period of crisis such as it has never experienced in the past.
These people are urged to economize or to content themselves with the little they have, but when the government wishes to take over the control of the country's credit it is urged not to interfere; when it is a question of putting the lid down on the possessors of great wealth, the government is asked to prevent their income from falling to the level of those of other classes; it is even requested to protect them because, otherwise, it would be equivalent to repudiation and would, therefore, harm the country's credit.

The Address-Mr. Bertrand
May I be so bold, sir, as to state that something must be done, that I belong to the younger generation that want to see, in the near future, Canada grow, become prosperous and blossom out into one of the finest countries of the world; but may I also point out that there is a growing feeling among the younger generation that its chances of success are slight and that in the struggle for life, it is denied the advantages enjoyed by the preceding generation because we are handicapped by the fact that capital is given more protection than the people. I therefore beseech the government not to neglect this serious problem but, with the help of the Bank of Canada, and its own authority, to find the best solution in the very near future.
A few moments ago, sir, I stated that I would give some details in connection with the problems of the farming class. I wish especially to deal with the subject from the Quebec and Ontario farmers' standpoint. I want first to state that many factors favour the Quebec farmers, notwithstanding the criticisms directed against the Taschereau regime which has been in office in this province for a number of years. May I point out that the taxes levied on the farmers of Ontario are 250 per cent higher than those levied on the farmers of Quebec. I reside in a county where only an imaginary line divides Quebec from Ontario; this permits us to draw comparisons which I could furnish to the house. However, this would not settle the problem which we have to face. I shall, therefore, refer only to the taxes which are levied on the farming class. In doing so I shall even go back thirty years the better to set forth the agricultural problem and the difficulty of remaining on the land. It has been contended that colonization could settle the unemployment problem. It is an easy matter to state that this question may be solved by settling a large number of our unemployed on colonization land. I reside in an exclusively farming county, yet we have never succeeded in the past in settling our farmers' sons on lands located in the northern parts of Quebec or Ontario. They had to abandon their farms because they were unable to meet their obligations and thus they increased the number of unemployed in small towns located close to their abandoned homes. This is a problem which needs the attention of all governments, both provincial and federal.
Continuing the comparisons, may I state that school, municipal and county taxes on 100 acres of land in Ontario in the Ottawa valley, amounted to $38 in 1901; to S60 in 1914; to $175 in 1930, and to $193 in 1935, That is, in 35 years, an increase of 500 per cent for these taxes alone.
The dominion government taxes are levied on the entire population; however, when so levied, the farmers are included. I shall therefore add these taxes to the figures that I have just quoted in order to point out the difficulties the farmers have to contend with.
The taxes levied by the dominion government, per capita, amounted to $8.72 in 1901; to $16.56 in 1914; to $36.01 in 1930, which is an increase of 120 per cent. The provincial taxes, per capita, amounted to $1.85 in 1901; in 1914, to $4.49; in 1930, to $17.50, an increase of 300 per cent in the last 30 years.
So as not to delay unduly this debate, I shall simply quote the prices on farm implements required by the farmer. In 1914. a six-foot mowing machine cost $43.50; in 1935, $97.50. A six-foot binder was worth $102 in 1914 and $205 in 1935. A hay cart cost $60 in 1914 and, in 1935, $122. A fifteen-discs sowing machine sold for $69 in 1914 and for $160 in 1935. These are increases ranging from 125 to 150 per cent in prices of farm implements.
The index figures of agricultural products were, in 1914, as follows:	farm products,
69; field products, 64; animal products, 79; making an average of 65-5. I have compared the figures between 1914, 1930 and 1935. In 1930, the same index figure was 86-6 and in 1935 it was 71. The value of farm products has therefore increased seven points on 64, or about 9 per cent, while the farmer's liabilities have increased 125 to 150 per cent on farm implements which he must necessarily purchase; 500, per cent in connection with school, municipal and [DOT] provincial taxes; 120 per cent as regards dominion taxes and 300 per cent for other taxes. It is therefore obvious that the situation in which the farmer is placed, at present is so difficult that we fear he will be unable to survive in our section of the country.
The economic situation with which the farmer is faced is somewhat as follows: one-third of our population barely receives 58 cents from the sale of their products instead of the dollar which they received, for instance, in 1929, the year when the index figure was 100. In other words, their purchasing power has dwindled to 58 per cent and, when these people purchase in their turn, they realize that prices of articles they require, far from having dropped proportionately to their purchasing power, are still 90 cents instead of a dollar. The result is that the farmer refuses to make purchases or that he buys less than two-thirds of what he requires. The depressing effect of this depre-
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis

ciated purchasing power on trade as a whole is so obvious that it is unnecessary further to stress the point. It is unquestionably obvious.
I shall close my remarks, Sir, by requesting the government to realize the necessity of helping the farming class as well as the other classes I have mentioned. Since 44 per cent of our population are farmers, it behooves us to find the means to relieve the farmers as soon as possible. The new markets abroad will certainly help us to dispose of our products; as the demand increases, better prices will prevail; we all agree on this point. That is why we wish to congratulate the government for what it has already achieved and further encourage it to take all necessary steps to reestablish equilibrium between every class of our community, in order that all classes of citizens inhabiting Canada may earn a livelihood and prosper in our country which we desire to see great, for the happiness of all.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, those of us who have sat in this corner of .the house during the past parliament and who are fortunate enough, if I may use the term, to be here again for this parliament, are in a fair position, I think, to watch the play and counteqplay that takes place in this chamber between the two great parties. My mind goes back to the special session of 1930, when a similar debate took place. The proceedings of the last few days remind me forcibly of the early days of the last parliament. Anyone not acquainted with the prominent actons concerned would be at a loss to know what the debate was about. The present leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) is using language almost identical with that used by the leader of the opposition in 1930, and the leader of the government (Mr. Mackenzie King) is using, possibly in a little different way, language similar to that used by the leader of the government in those days. The results of the election were analyzed; it was assumed that because the Conservative party had a majority in the house in 1930 the people of Canada had endorsed the Conservative party. Now it is assumed that because the Liberal party have an overwhelming majority in parliament the people of Canada have endorsed Liberal principles. I think the assumption is not true in either case. The people of Canada have no idea what Conservative principles are or what Liberal principles are, because neither the Liberals nor the Conservatives have taken the trouble to lay before the people what their principles are and what the consequences of their principles would be if they Were put into effect.

May I in a friendly way say to the members of the government party that they should not delude themselves with the idea that they are here because the people have endorsed Liberal principles. They are not here on that account; they are here because the last government failed to do what the people of Canada thought it should do, and what the government had said it would do. The votes cast in the last election for candidates of the Liberal party were not necessarily votes for Liberalism; they were votes against the Conservative party. They were negative votes. The people did not know and do not know now what the Liberal party had to offer them. But they did know what they had suffered during that period of five years, and as a protest against that, even a negative protest, they voted, almost -as a matter of habit, for the other party, as alternatively they had voted election in and election out ever since 1867. So may I say to the leader of the government that the same fate awaits the Liberal government that overtook the Conservative government, if within the next feiw years they do not put into effect policies that will enable the people to avail themselves of the great actual and potential wealth of the country.
We heard during the last parliament a great deal about promises. The leader of the last government carried out at least one of his promises; he said he was (going to end unemployment or perish in the attempt, and he has .perished. It was not necessary for my Liberal friends to make promises; the .people knew what had happened to them, and all they were waiting for was a chance to state their protest in the only way available to them. In order to impress that more clearly upon the minds of my Liberal friends may I draw their attention to the present plight of the Liberal government in the province of British Columbia.
That government was elected with possibly not quite but relatively as large a majority of members in the legislature as was the Liberal government here in Ottawa. After two years in office that same government is afraid to hold by-elections which by the laws of the province are due, because they are convinced that defeat is awaiting them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Who is going to defeat them?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
They, themselves, will be the cause of their defeat, coupled with the activities of the party in British Columbia that had the largest vote at the last election. My hon. friend knows which party that was. If he will read the Liberal organ of the city of

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis
Vancouver he will learn who is going to defeat the government. Let me read from the Vancouver Sun an editorial of recent date:
With five Liberal members British Columbia will have an audible voice in the new Liberal government

That is, the Liberal government in Ottawa-
-but that voice will not shut out the fact that more than 89,000 people voted in anger and protest against their own interests for the socialists. Protest against what? Protest against Premier T. D. Pattullo who was returned to, office on a disregarded "work and wages" program, and has since held his office under flagrant false pretences.
That is not a Cooperative Commonwealth publication. It is a Liberal paper supporting a Liberal government in the province of British Columbia.
As I listened last night to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) complaining about the tactics used against him in the province of Quebec my sympathy went out to him, because the same tactics were used ini the province of British Columbia. In that province however it was not the Conservative party but the party to which the minister belongs which stooped to those unworthy actions. It was the Liberal party that stooped to anything. Nothing was too dirty; nothing was too mean; nothing was too sordid if it would bring them votes. When the minister is complaining about the tactics of the Conservative party in Quebec let him try to improve the tactics of the Liberal party in British Columbia, and we may get somewhere.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Where did the Liberal party in British Columbia resort to the tactics to which the hon. member has referred? I should like to know that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The hon. member lives in the far north; I believe he lives in the city of Prince Rupert, or somewhere in that vicinity, and at a point very difficult to reach and very difficult to get away from. Possibly the news has not yet reached Prince Rupert, but I have no doubt it will reach that point in due time. We are told the Minister of Justice was accused of being a communist and tearing down the steeples and walking on the crucifixes; I say to him that the very same accusations were made in the city of Vancouver. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeqr) who is not now in his seat was the saviour-that is, outside of the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) -the man who saved the country singlehanded from the communists. He arrived here on a margin of six votes. His efforts reminded me of those of Horatius at the bridge.
But this time while there was one other man who would hold the bridge with the hon. member, they could not find three. However that did not prevent the Liberal party from helping the communists in Vancouver East.
I am told that the communist candidate in Vancouver East did not put in an account of his election expenses, and I understand his reason for refraining was, that the Liberal party had provided the funds and that it was up to them to put in the expense account.
Quebec is not the only province in Canada where racial questions are raised. A few days ago our representative at Geneva said he was glad to say that we did not have any minority problems in Canada. That is not true. We do have racial and minority questions. An article appearing in the Canadian Forum of December, 1935, and written by Professor H. F. Angus of the university of British Columbia is in point. So far as I know Professor Angus is not a .member of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. I believe, that he is a member of or adheres to the Liberal party. In any case I know he went into the province of Alberta either for or with the Liberal party in an attempt to stem the tide of Social Credit during the provincial election campaign. The article is headed Liberalism Stoops to Conquer. Although I am not going to weary the house with quotations, because I shall have something further to say on this point at another time, I shall quote what were indicated in British Columbia as being Liberal policies, and will ask the Liberal government here in Ottawa if they approve of what I shall indicate, and if they believe that that kind of thing is going to improve Canada's relations with the rest of the world. The article headed Liberalism Stoops to Conquer is in part as follows:
The sophisticated view that political parties are cynical conspiracies to capture or retain political power received some confirmation from the action of the Liberal candidates in British Columbia, who published large advertisements informing the electors that there were 50,000 Asiatics in the province and that the C.C.F. was pledged to extend the franchise to them. "A vote for any C.C.F. candidate is a vote to give the Chinaman and' the Japanese the same voting right that you have."
If a Chinaman or Japanese is a Canadian citizen, born in Canada, is it British justice or is it Liberalism that he be denied the same rights as we have, simply because the colour of his skin or the slant of his eyes may be different?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Do you mean that Chinese
from the orient should have the same rights as whites in Canada?
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Absolutely-and not only Chinese and Japanese, but every man and woman to whom we extend the rights of citizenship. What do rights of citizenship mean if they do not imply the right to take part in the government of the country? These people are paying federal taxes, provincial taxes and municipal taxes. They were bom and are living in Canada. They have fought for this country, and I believe it is the British viewpoint that regardless of the colour of their skin or who their forebears or ancestors were they should be treated in Canada the same as every other Canadian citizen. But more of that later on.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Would my hon. friend be in favour of oriental immigration to Canada?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That is not the question now. I have a resolution on the order paper dealing with that, and I shall discuss it then. But I am speaking now of the tactics of the Liberal party in raising racial prejudices in the province of British Columbia. When my friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), who I believe is a good democrat in the best sense of the term, and believes I think in British justice and fair play, complains of the tactics of the Conservative party in the province of Quebec, he should see to it that his own friends are not following the same kind of tactics in British Columbia or any other province. I quote again from the Liberal campaign advertisements:
A vote for any C.C.F. candidate is a vote to give the Chinaman and the Japanese the same voting right that you have.
The article goes on:
Against this enormity the Liberals undertook to protect the state.
Here is another quotation from the Liberal campaign literature:
. A vote for the Liberal candidate in your riding is a vote against oriental enfranchisement. The Liberal party is opposed to giving the orientals the vote.
Note that, sir-the Liberal party is opposed to giving the orientals the vote. That is the Liberal party sitting to-day on the other side of this house and up in the corner to your left, Mr. Speaker; the Liberal party which is the government of Canada at the moment. What a wonderful help such a statement will be in their negotiations with Japan to improve trade relations between the two countries.

At six o'clock the house adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order.
